(1) maize yield variability is mainly driven by the concentration of production in a single region of above-average yield variability; (2) rice yield variability is mainly determined by the concentration of croplands in regions of below average variability.
the global yield variability of maize is driven by a single region (the North American corn belt), that of wheat by a few regions, and that of soybean and rice by a large number of regions.
the spatial distribution of crop yields is a major factor determining interannual crop yield variability, and that this distribution varies across crops.

the spatial distribution and temporal stability of crop production, and how these two factors affect the global food system.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spatial allocation of croplands is the most important driver of global crop yield inter-annual variability.
global crop production is not very stable because of the concentration of croplands in a few world regions with large interannual variability.

The main takeaway from our work is that
global crop yield inter-annual variability is driven not only by the geographical allocation of cultivated lands, but also by the spatial distribution of the between-year variability across regions.
, in the case of maize, global production is not stable because of the concentration of croplands in one region, and not because of the high variability of yields in this region.
global food security could be enhanced through a more even distribution of cultivated areas across regions with different levels of yield interannual variability.
